scenario: AITA for not jumping up and helping my parents bring in the groceries? I'm an adult and I pay rent if that helps. | I'm 33 years old and I've pretty much always lived with my parents. To me there's no shame in it because it's super cheap (they charge me $200, which honestly would be market rate where we live) and it has everything I want and need without the hassle of having to look for a new place to live. We get along most of the time but honestly I just avoid them. Recently the toilet flooded in my bathroom which means they are having to remodel my section of the house so we "run into" each other a lot more than when I used to lock myself in my room most of the time. Well today my parents went to Costco. When they got home I was sitting on the couch playing Apex and my mom asked me to get up and help them bring in groceries. I told her in a minute. I was honestly too into my game to notice that they made several trips back and forth and finally my dad told me to get my ass up. I told him I would in a minute. He said a minute is now and grabbed the controller out of my hand. It turned into a huge shouting match and now they are checking into a hotel and expecting me to have a place to live by Friday (which is basically impossible). Of course they brought up my younger brother who is married with two kids and was just promoted at his job. They have their golden child of course but to throw his shit in my face is bullshit. I mean I guess I could have gotten up and helped them but to me because I pay rent that gives me the privilege to pretty much say no when they ask me for stuff like helping with groceries or yard work. Am I the asshole in this situation?

It’s great that wearing a suit and tie makes you feel confident—that’s a powerful connection between appearance and self-perception! Many people experience the same boost in confidence when dressing formally, and there’s actually some science behind it.

### Why It Works:
1. **Power Posing & Nonverbal Cues** – Studies (like Amy Cuddy’s research on "power posing") suggest that wearing formal attire can subtly influence how others perceive you, which in turn can make *you* feel more authoritative or capable. Even if it’s just psychological, the effect can be real.
2. **Ritual & Routine** – Dressing up can act as a mental cue, signaling to your brain that you’re entering a "high-stakes" or "professional" mode, which can sharpen focus and reduce anxiety.
3. **Social Norms** – In many professional settings, suits and ties are associated with competence, respect, and seriousness. When you align with those expectations, it can reinforce your own belief in your ability to succeed.
4. **Body Language Feedback** – Standing taller, holding your head high, and moving with purpose (often unconsciously when dressed formally) can amplify feelings of confidence.

### Potential Caveats:
- **Comfort Matters** – If the suit feels restrictive or uncomfortable, it might undermine confidence instead. Find a fit that’s both polished and *you*.
- **Context Matters** – In creative or casual environments, formal wear might feel out of place. Confidence isn’t tied to one style—it’s about authenticity.
- **Self-Fulfilling Prophecy** – If you *believe* the suit makes you confident, it likely will—even if others don’t notice. That’s the power of mindset!

### Pro Tip:
Pair the suit with a **posture check** (shoulders back, chin up) and **mindset reinforcement** (e.g., "I own this space"). The combo can create a compound effect.
